HOME ECONOMICS
PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
FIRST TERM
WEEK 4
PRIMARY 6
THEME -
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC: MEAL PLANNING
Meal planning means making a careful plan of meals with adequate balanced diet for different situation such as for an individual, family and friends, restaurants, wedding, naming, birthday, anniversary, festival and so on.
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. explain the meaning of meal planning;
2. identify three major meals of the day;
3. identify the right foods for each meal;
4. plan simple breakfast, lunch and supper/dinner.
ENTRY BEHAVIOR
The pupils can differentiate between breakfast, lunch and dinner.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Charts on food nutrients;
2. Charts on food groups;
3. Charts on adequate diet.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Course Book
All Relevant Material
Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Food nutrients are substance needed in the body for growth, reproduce and survival.
CLASSIFICATION OF FOODS - FUNCTIONS - SOURCES
1. CARBOHYDRATES
Carbohydrates are energy given food and found in food like rice, noodles, bread and other products that have grains.
2. FATS
Fats are for growth and function normally and help with tissue growth. They are found in foods like meat, fish, whole eggs, vegetables, nuts.
3. MINERALS
Minerals are Calcium, Iron, Magnesium, Potassium and Zinc. Minerals can be found meat, fish, poultry, grains.
4. PROTEINS
Proteins are for growth, maintain or repair tissues and found in food like rice, beans, dairy products, fish, meat, eggs.
5. VITAMINS
Vitamins help to regulate and boost immune system of the body. They can be found in almost any product on the earth.
6. WATER
Water support life and needed on regular basis.
MEANING OF MEAL PLANNING
Meal planning is the planning of major nutritional meals to be eaten in a day, week or month.
This planning puts in consideration the appropriate nutrition for the breakfast, lunch and dinner.
IMPORTANCE OF MEAL PLANNING
1. It saves time, energy and money.
2. It adds nutritional value to meals.
3. It is required for healthy living.
4. It reduces stress and anxiety.
5. It reduces wastage.
6. It takes care of personal like and dislike.
7. It helps in budgeting.
8. It gives room for variety.
9. It creates awareness.
THREE MAJOR MEALS OF THE DAY
1. Breakfast
2. Lunch
3. Dinner
TYPES OF FOODS FOR EACH MEAL OF THE DAY
BREAKFAST
Breakfast is the first meals of the day usually eaten in the morning.
For examples,
Ogi (Pap), Bread and Eggs, Bread with butter and Tea, Golden Morn, Boiled Plantains and Stew, Nigerian Salad, Rice and Beans, fried plantains and Beans, and so on.
LUNCH
Breakfast is the second meals of the day usually eaten in the afternoon.
For examples,
Amala with Fish stew and Ewedu, Fufu with Efo Riro (vegetable stew), Jollof Rice and Dodo (fried plantain) with meat or chicken stew, Iyan (pounded yam) with Egusi stew, White Rice with moi moi and stewed fish or fried meat or chicken, Semolina or Amala with Ogbonno and Bitter Leaf stew.
DINNER
Dinner is the last meals of the day usually eaten in the night.
For examples,
Rice with Efo Riro (vegetable stew), Fried Rice with coleslaw, fried chicken, Eko with meat or chicken stew, Boiled Plantains with meat or chicken stew or vegetable stew, Tuwo (ground rice) with meat stew.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. Revises the previous lesson based on the pupil’s knowledge or experience.
Pupil’s Activities - Participate actively in the lesson revision.
2. Asks write in their note the meals taken in the last two days.
3. Uses their responses to introduce and explain the meaning food nutrition and classes of food.
Pupil’s Activities - Explain the meaning food nutrition and state the classes of food.
4. Leads pupils to recall and state the sources of nutrients.
Pupil’s Activities - Recall the classes of foods and their functions.
5. Displays chart showing meal menu for a week.
6. Leads a discussion on the meaning of meal planning and its importance.
Pupil’s Activities - Identify the meal menu and participate actively in the discussion.
7. Uses the menu chart to explain major major meals of the day.
8. Asks pupils to suggest appropriate meals for the breakfast, lunch and dinner.
Pupil’s Activities - State the appropriate meal for the breakfast, lunch and dinner.
9. Homework - Asks pupils to design a week meal timetable.
Pupil’s Activities - Design a week meal timetable.
10. Check and correct the unbalanced meal in their meal plan.
Pupil’s Activities - Take correction, redesign and display meal plan.
CONCLUSION
- To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
- Next Lesson -
LESSON EVALUATION
Ask pupil to:
1. explain the meaning of food nutrition.
2. state 5 classes of food with appropriate examples.
3. explain the meaning of meal planning;
4. Differentiate between the major meals.
5. mention 5 importance of meal planning.

By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. explain the meaning of wise buying and spending;
2. identify items of needs and wants;
3. state the advantages and ways of spending wisely.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Wise buying is knowing exactly what to buy, when and where to buy at the right price without any regret in the future.
Wise spending is the decision we make on what we spend money on.
ADVANTAGES OF WISE SPENDING AND BUYING
1. Save money
2. Save time
3. Increase in savings
4. Enable you to get more goods and services for lesser price
5. Reduce unnecessary buying and spending.
LESSON 2 - HOW/WAYS TO SPEND MONEY WISELY
1. Listing items for purchase,
2. Price comparison,
3. Products comparison,
4. Bulk buying,
5. Shop alone,
6. Learn how to negotiate,
7. Don’t fool by advertisements,
8. Avoid online shopping except for price comparison.

1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Ask pupils where to buy goods at cheaper rate.
3. Ask pupils, why should we buy there.
Pupil’s Activities - State reasons why we should buy goods at wholesale shops.
4. Introduces the lesson and explain the meaning of wise spending.
5. Leads to state the ways of wise spending.
Pupil’s Activities - State some of the ways of spending money wisely.

Pupil’s Activities - Participate actively in the market prices.

NEXT LESSON

Ask pupils to:
1. explain the meaning of wise spending.
2. make a list of four market items to buy with cost estimates.
3. state three advantages of comparing prices.

topics.content:
REASONS FOR CLEANING THE HOUSE, CLASSROOM AND THE ENVIRONMENT AND GUIDELINES FOR CLEANING THE HOUSE AND ITS SURROUNDINGS
HOME ECONOMICS
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 1
THEME - PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - First Term, Second Term and Third Term Home Economics Plan Lesson Notes and Scheme of Work for Primary 5 (Basic 5)
TOPIC - REASONS FOR CLEANING THE HOUSE, CLASSROOM AND THE ENVIRONMENT
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of a Healthy Home Environment
3. Meaning of Cleaning and Reasons for Cleaning the House, Classroom, and Environment
4. Guidelines for Cleaning the Home and Its Surroundings
5. Cleaning the Classroom
6. Importance of Keeping the Environment Clean
7. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
8. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a healthy home environment.
2. Explain the meaning of cleaning.
3. State the reasons for cleaning the house, classroom, and environment.
4. Mention guidelines for cleaning the home, classroom and its surroundings.
5. Explain the importance of keeping the home and environment clean.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about personal hygiene and proper care of the home.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how to maintain a clean, safe, and healthy home, classroom, and environment.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Broom, Mop and bucket, Dustpan, Duster, Cleaning brush, Waste bin, Cleaning agents
2. Pictures or charts showing a clean and dirty environment
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
A healthy home environment is clean, safe, and comfortable for people to live and carry out their daily activities. However, dirt, waste, germs, and pests can make the home, classroom, and surroundings unhealthy.
Regular cleaning helps to prevent diseases, control pests, reduce bad odours, and keep the environment safe and attractive.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and reasons for cleaning the house, classroom, and environment, as well as guidelines for cleaning the home and its surroundings.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF A HEALTHY HOME ENVIRONMENT
A healthy home environment is a clean, safe, and comfortable place where people live and carry out their daily activities without unnecessary health risks.
MEANING OF CLEANING
Cleaning is the process of removing dirt, dust, stains, waste, and unwanted materials from the home, classroom, and surroundings.
REASONS FOR CLEANING THE HOUSE, CLASSROOM, AND ENVIRONMENT
Cleaning is important because it:
1. Prevents diseases by removing dirt and germs.
2. Keeps the environment neat and attractive.
3. Prevents bad odours caused by waste and dirt.
4. Controls pests such as flies, cockroaches, and rodents.
5. Provides a safe environment and reduces accidents.
6. Improves comfort for people living or working in the environment.
7. Protects furniture and household items from damage caused by dirt.
8. Promotes good hygiene habits among children and adults.
LESSON 2 - GUIDELINES FOR CLEANING THE HOME AND ITS SURROUNDINGS
1. Open windows and doors where appropriate to allow fresh air into the house.
2. Gather cleaning materials before starting the cleaning.
3. Remove waste and rubbish and dispose them properly.
4. Dust surfaces such as tables, shelves, and furniture.
5. Sweep or vacuum the floors to remove dirt and dust.
6. Mop the floor with clean water and a suitable cleaning agent.
7. Clean toilets and bathrooms regularly.
8. Wash cooking utensils and kitchen surfaces properly.
9. Keep the surroundings free from stagnant water and waste.
10. Clean drainage channels and ensure they are not blocked.
11. Store cleaning materials safely after use.
12. Wash hands thoroughly after cleaning.
LESSON 3 - GUIDELINES FOR CLEANING THE CLASSROOM
A clean classroom should have:
1. Clean floors and walls.
2. Dust-free desks and chairs.
3. Clean windows and doors.
5. Properly arranged furniture.
6. A clean and covered waste bin.
7. Good ventilation.
8. Clean and safe surroundings.
IMPORTANCE OF KEEPING THE ENVIRONMENT CLEAN
A clean environment helps to:
1. Reduce the spread of diseases.
2. Prevent pest infestation.
3. Reduce accidents.
4. Improve concentration and learning.
5. Promote comfort and well-being.
6. Make the home and school attractive.
7. Encourage responsible behaviour.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is a healthy home environment?
A. A clean, safe, and comfortable place
B. A dirty and unsafe place
C. A noisy place
D. A crowded place
2. What is cleaning?
A. Adding more dirt
B. Removing dirt and waste
C. Storing waste indoors
D. Spreading dust
3. Which of the following is used for sweeping the floor?
A. Spoon
B. Plate
C. Cup
D. Broom
4. Why should the house be cleaned regularly?
A. To encourage pests
B. To increase dirt
C. To prevent diseases
D. To create bad odour
5. Which of the following is a good cleaning practice?
A. Leaving waste on the floor
B. Disposing of waste properly
C. Blocking drainage channels
D. Allowing stagnant water around the house
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. A healthy home environment should be clean, safe, and ______.
7. ______ is the process of removing dirt, dust, and waste.
8. A ______ can be used to sweep the floor.
9. Proper cleaning helps to control ______ such as flies and cockroaches.
10. Waste should be disposed of ______.
C. True or False
11. Cleaning helps to prevent the spread of diseases. ______
12. A dirty classroom provides a healthy learning environment. ______
13. Stagnant water should be removed from the surroundings. ______
14. Cleaning can help to control pests. ______
15. Cleaning materials should be stored safely after use. ______
D. Matching
16. Cleaning - A. Removes dust from surfaces
17. Broom - B. Sweeps the floor
18. Duster - C. Holds waste
19. Waste bin - D. Cleans the floor with water
20. Mop - E. Removes dirt and unwanted materials
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. D 4. C 5. B
6. Comfortable
7. Cleaning
8. Broom
9. Pests
10. Properly
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. True
15. True
16. Cleaning - E. Removes dirt and unwanted materials
17. Broom - B. Sweeps the floor
18. Duster - A. Removes dust from surfaces
19. Waste bin - C. Holds waste
20. Mop - D. Cleans the floor with water
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a healthy home environment is a clean, safe, and comfortable place. They learned that cleaning involves removing dirt, dust, waste, and unwanted materials from the house, classroom, and surroundings.
They also learned that regular cleaning prevents diseases, controls pests, reduces bad odours, improves safety, and keeps the environment neat and attractive. Proper cleaning involves sweeping, dusting, mopping, disposing of waste properly, and keeping the surroundings clean.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What happens when a house is not cleaned regularly?
- Why should we keep our classroom and surroundings clean?
The teacher explains that cleanliness helps to prevent diseases, control pests, reduce bad odours, and make the environment safe and comfortable.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention reasons why the home, classroom, and surroundings should be kept clean.
Step 2: Meaning of Healthy Home Environment and Cleaning
The teacher explains that a healthy home environment is a clean, safe, and comfortable place for people to live.
The teacher also explains that cleaning is the process of removing dirt, dust, waste, and unwanted materials from the home, classroom, and surroundings.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of a healthy home environment and cleaning in their own words.
Step 3: Reasons for Cleaning the House, Classroom and Environment
The teacher explains that cleaning:
- Prevents diseases.
- Controls pests such as flies and cockroaches.
- Reduces bad odours.
- Keeps the environment neat and attractive.
- Prevents accidents.
- Makes the environment safe and comfortable.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the reasons for cleaning the home, classroom, and environment.
Step 4: Cleaning Tools and Their Uses
The teacher displays or mentions common cleaning tools and their uses:
- Broom: Sweeps the floor.
- Mop: Cleans the floor with water.
- Duster: Removes dust from surfaces.
- Dustpan: Collects dirt and rubbish.
- Brush: Scrubs surfaces.
- Waste bin: Holds waste.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the cleaning tools and state their uses.
Step 5: Guidelines for Cleaning the Home and Surroundings
The teacher explains the guidelines for proper cleaning:
- Gather the necessary cleaning materials.
- Open windows and doors where appropriate for ventilation.
- Remove waste and dispose of it properly.
- Dust furniture and other surfaces.
- Sweep the floor.
- Mop the floor with clean water and a suitable cleaning agent.
- Clean the kitchen, bathroom, and toilet regularly.
- Remove stagnant water and keep drainage channels clear.
- Store cleaning materials safely after use.
- Wash hands after cleaning.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state and demonstrate some of the guidelines for cleaning.
Step 6: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Mention five reasons for cleaning the home and surroundings.
- Group 2: Mention five cleaning tools and their uses.
- Group 3: State five guidelines for cleaning the home.
- Group 4: State five ways of keeping the classroom clean.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 7: Practical Demonstration
The teacher demonstrates how to clean a room by dusting surfaces, sweeping the floor, collecting waste, and mopping the floor. The teacher emphasises proper handling and safe storage of cleaning materials.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and practise the cleaning activities under the teacher’s guidance.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning and reasons for cleaning the house, classroom, and environment, as well as the guidelines for proper cleaning. The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions to assess their understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups and summarise what they have learned.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Healthy Home Environment: Tools and Agents for Cleaning the Home and Its Surroundings, and the Process of Cleaning the Home Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 2 Home Economics
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is a healthy home environment?
2. What is cleaning?
3. Mention five reasons for cleaning the house and its surroundings.
4. State five guidelines for cleaning the home.
5. Mention four cleaning tools and state their uses.

topics.content:
TOOLS AND AGENTS FOR CLEANING THE HOME AND ITS SURROUNDINGS AND THE PROCESS OF CLEANING THE HOME
HOME ECONOMICS
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 2
THEME - PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Healthy Home Environment: Meaning and Reasoning for Cleaning the House, Classroom and the Environment and Guidelines for Cleaning Home and Its Surroundings Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 1 Home Economics
TOPIC - TOOLS AND AGENTS FOR CLEANING THE HOME AND ITS SURROUNDINGS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Cleaning Tools and Agents
3. Process of Cleaning the Home
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Identify common tools used for cleaning the home and its surroundings.
2. State the uses of different cleaning tools.
3. Mention common cleaning agents and their uses.
4. Explain the process of cleaning the home.
5. Demonstrate proper cleaning practices.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the meaning and reasons for cleaning the house, classroom, and environment.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to cleaning tools, cleaning agents, and the process of cleaning the home.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Cleaning Tools - Broom, Mop, Duster, Dustpan, Scrubbing brush, Sponge, Bucket
2. Cleaning Agents - Soap, Detergent, Disinfectant
3. Pictures or charts of cleaning tools and agents
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Different tools and cleaning agents are used to keep the home and its surroundings clean. Brooms, mops, dusters, brushes, soap, detergents, and disinfectants help to remove dirt, dust, stains, and germs.
Proper cleaning also requires following the correct steps, from gathering materials and removing waste to dusting, sweeping, mopping, and storing cleaning materials safely.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the tools and agents used for cleaning the home and its surroundings and the process of cleaning the home.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF CLEANING TOOLS
Cleaning tools are objects used to remove dirt, dust, stains, and waste from the home and its surroundings.
CLEANING TOOLS AND THEIR USES
1. Broom - Sweeps floors and surroundings
2. Mop - Cleans floors with water
3. Duster - Removes dust from surfaces
4. Dustpan - Collects dirt and rubbish
5. Scrubbing brush - Scrubs floors and other surfaces
6. Toilet brush - Cleans the toilet bowl
7. Bucket - Holds water during cleaning
8. Sponge - Cleans and wipes surfaces
LESSON 2 - MEANING OF CLEANING AGENTS
Cleaning agents are substances used to remove dirt, stains, grease, and germs from surfaces.
EXAMPLES OF CLEANING AGENTS AND THEIR USES
1. Soap - Used for washing and removing dirt.
2. Detergent - Used for washing clothes, floors, and surfaces.
3. Disinfectant - Used to reduce or kill harmful microorganisms on suitable surfaces.
4. Bleach - Used for disinfecting and removing stains when used appropriately.
5. Scouring powder - Used for removing stubborn dirt and stains from suitable hard surfaces.
LESSON 3 - PROCESS OF CLEANING THE HOME
1. Prepare the Cleaning Materials - Gather the required cleaning tools and agents before starting.
2. Open Windows and Doors - Open windows and doors where appropriate to allow fresh air into the rooms.
3. Remove Waste - Collect rubbish and dispose of it properly.
4. Dust Surfaces - Dust furniture, shelves, windowsills, and other surfaces.
5. Sweep the Floor - Sweep the floor carefully to remove dust, dirt, and debris.
6. Scrub or Mop the Floor - Use a suitable cleaning agent and clean water to scrub or mop the floor.
7. Clean the Kitchen and Bathroom - Wash sinks, kitchen surfaces, bathrooms, and toilets properly.
8. Clean the Surroundings - Remove waste, weeds, and stagnant water from around the home. Keep drainage channels clear.
9. Arrange the Home - Arrange furniture and household items neatly after cleaning.
10. Store Cleaning Materials Safely - Wash and store cleaning tools properly and keep cleaning agents out of children’s reach.
11. Wash Hands - Wash hands thoroughly with soap and clean water after completing the cleaning activity.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Which of the following is a cleaning tool?
A. Spoon
B. Plate
C. Cup
D. Broom
2. What is a mop mainly used for?
A. Dusting furniture
B. Cleaning floors with water
C. Collecting rubbish
D. Scrubbing the toilet
3. Which cleaning agent is commonly used for washing and removing dirt?
A. Soap
B. Sand
C. Oil
D. Kerosene
4. What should be done first when cleaning the home?
A. Gather the cleaning materials
B. Mop the floor
C. Arrange the furniture
D. Store the cleaning tools

A. Duster
B. Mop
C. Dustpan
D. Sponge
B. Fill in the Gaps

7. A ______ is used to remove dust from surfaces.
8. ______ is a cleaning agent used for washing and removing dirt.

C. True or False

SUMMARY
Pupils learned that cleaning tools are objects used to remove dirt, dust, and waste from the home and its surroundings. Examples include broom, mop, duster, dustpan, brush, sponge, and bucket.
They also learned that cleaning agents are substances used to remove dirt, stains, grease, and germs. Examples include soap, detergent, disinfectant, and bleach.
The process of cleaning involves gathering materials, removing waste, dusting, sweeping, scrubbing or mopping, cleaning the surroundings, arranging the home, and storing cleaning materials safely.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What cleaning tools do you know?
- What is a broom used for?
- Why do we use soap and detergent when cleaning?
The teacher explains that different tools and agents are used to remove dirt, dust, stains, and germs from the home and its surroundings.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention cleaning tools and agents they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Cleaning Tools and Examples
The teacher explains that cleaning tools are objects used to remove dirt, dust, stains, and waste.
- Examples include broom, mop, duster, dustpan, scrubbing brush, toilet brush, bucket, and sponge.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the cleaning tools and state their uses.
Step 3: Cleaning Agents and Their Uses

- Remove waste and dispose of it properly.
- Dust furniture and other surfaces.

- Scrub or mop the floor.
- Clean the kitchen, bathroom, and toilet.
- Clean the surroundings.
- Arrange the home neatly.
- Store cleaning tools and agents safely.

4. Mention healthy eating practices.
5. State five importance of healthy eating.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about food nutrients and the importance of a healthy home environment.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how to plan balanced meals and make healthy food choices.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People need different types of food to provide energy, support growth, and maintain good health. However, eating without proper planning may result in an unbalanced diet or poor food choices.
Meal planning helps families decide what meals to prepare and ensures that different nutrients are included in the diet. Healthy eating involves choosing a variety of nutritious foods in the right amounts.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and importance of meal planning and the importance of healthy eating.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF MEAL PLANNING
Meal planning is the process of deciding in advance the meals to be prepared and eaten over a particular period, taking into consideration the nutritional needs, age, health, preferences, available food, and income of the family.
A good meal plan should provide a balanced diet containing the major nutrients needed by the body.
IMPORTANCE OF MEAL PLANNING
Meal planning helps to:
1. Provide balanced and nutritious meals.
2. Ensure that the family gets different types of nutrients.
3. Save time and energy when preparing meals.
4. Reduce food wastage.
5. Control food expenses.
6. Make good use of available food.
7. Provide variety in meals.
8. Help the family eat meals at regular times.
LESSON 2 - Meaning of Healthy Eating
Healthy eating means choosing and eating a variety of foods in the right amounts to provide the nutrients and energy needed for growth, development, and good health.
Examples of Healthy Eating Practices
1. Eat a variety of foods.
2. Eat fruits and vegetables regularly.
3. Choose foods that provide protein, carbohydrates, healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals.
4. Drink enough clean water.
5. Limit excessive intake of foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats.
6. Eat meals at appropriate times.
7. Maintain proper food hygiene.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF HEALTHY EATING
Healthy eating:
1. Promotes proper growth and development.
2. Provides energy for daily activities.
3. Helps the body fight diseases.
4. Supports strong bones, muscles, and teeth.
5. Helps maintain a healthy body weight.
6. Improves concentration and learning.
7. Supports the proper functioning of body organs.
8. Promotes general well-being.

SUMMARY
Pupils learned that meal planning is the process of deciding in advance the meals to be prepared and eaten. They learned that good meal planning helps to provide balanced meals, save time and money, reduce food wastage, and provide variety in meals.
They also learned that healthy eating means choosing and eating a variety of nutritious foods in the right amounts. Healthy eating provides nutrients and energy, supports growth and development, helps the body fight diseases, and promotes good health.

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Identify the three major meals of the day.
2. Explain the meaning of breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
3. Give examples of foods that can be eaten at each major meal.
4. Mention factors to be considered when planning meals.
5. Explain the importance of considering these factors when planning meals.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the meaning of meal planning and the importance of healthy eating.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about the three major meals of the day and factors to consider when planning meals.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People eat different meals at different times of the day to provide the body with energy and nutrients. The three major meals of the day are breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
When planning meals, factors such as age, health, income, food availability, nutritional value, food preferences, number of people, and activity level should be considered.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the three major meals of the day and the factors to be considered when planning meals.
THREE MAJOR MEALS OF THE DAY
The three major meals of the day are breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
1. Breakfast
Breakfast is the first main meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning. It provides energy needed for school, work, and other morning activities.
Examples:
- Bread and egg
- Pap and akara
- Oatmeal and milk
- Yam and egg
2. Lunch
Lunch is the main meal eaten around the middle of the day. It helps to replace energy used during morning activities.
Examples:
- Rice and vegetables
- Beans and plantain
- Yam and vegetable sauce
- Eba and soup
3. Dinner
Dinner is the evening meal, usually eaten later in the day. It should provide needed nutrients without being unnecessarily heavy.
Examples:
- Rice and vegetables
- Beans and plantain
- Yam and egg sauce
- Eba and soup
FACTORS TO BE CONSIDERED WHEN PLANNING MEALS
The following factors should be considered when planning meals:
1. Age: Different age groups have different nutritional needs.
2. Health condition: The meal should suit the health needs of family members.
3. Income: Meals should be planned according to the family’s available money.
4. Availability of food: Available foods in the locality and season should be considered.
5. Nutritional value: Meals should contain the nutrients needed by the body.
6. Food preferences: Likes and dislikes of family members should be considered.
7. Number of people: The quantity of food should be enough for the number of people to be served.
8. Occupation and activity level: People who engage in more physical activities may require more energy.
9. Time available: Meals should be planned according to the time available for preparation.
10. Variety: Different foods should be included to make meals interesting and provide different nutrients.
IMPORTANCE OF CONSIDERING FACTORS WHEN PLANNING MEALS
1. It provides balanced nutrition: It helps ensure that meals contain the nutrients needed for growth and good health.
2. It meets individual needs: Age, health condition and activity level help determine the type and amount of food a person needs.
3. It saves money: Considering income helps families plan meals they can afford.
4. It uses available foods: It helps in choosing foods that are easily available in the home or community.
5. It prevents food waste: Planning according to the number of people helps prepare the right quantity of food.
6. It meets food preferences: Considering people’s likes, dislikes and food habits makes meals more acceptable.
7. It provides variety: It helps prevent eating the same type of food regularly.
8. It waves time and energy: Proper planning makes food preparation easier and more organised.
9. It promotes good health: Considering health conditions helps avoid foods that may be harmful to a person.
10. It provides enough energy: Considering occupation and activity level helps ensure that meals provide enough energy for daily activities.

17. Lunch - B. Ability to pay for food

SUMMARY
Pupils learned that the three major meals of the day are breakfast, lunch, and dinner. They learned that breakfast is eaten in the morning, lunch is eaten around the middle of the day, and dinner is eaten in the evening.
They also learned that factors such as age, health condition, income, food availability, nutritional value, food preferences, number of people, and activity level should be considered when planning meals. Considering these factors helps to provide balanced meals, save money and time, reduce food wastage, meet individual needs, and promote good health.

- What food do you eat in the afternoon?

The teacher explains that people eat different meals at different times of the day. Proper meal planning helps us choose suitable and nutritious foods.

THE EFFECTS OF WRONG MEAL PLANNING, EATING HABITS AND MENU CARD
HOME ECONOMICS
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 6
THEME - PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Three Major Meals of the Day and Factors to be Considered in Planning Meals Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 5 Home Economics

1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Effects of Wrong Meal Planning
3. Meaning and Importance of Good Eating Habits
4. Meaning and Importance of Menu Card
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of wrong meal planning.
2. Identify the effects of wrong meal planning.
3. Explain the meaning of eating habits.
4. Identify good and poor eating habits and their effects.
5. Explain the meaning and importance of a menu card.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the three major meals of the day and the factors to consider when planning meals.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils about the effects of wrong meal planning, eating habits, and the meaning and importance of a menu card.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of healthy and unhealthy meals
2. Sample menu cards
3. Food pictures or samples
4. Meal-planning chart
5. Food group chart

Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.

2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People need to plan their meals properly and develop good eating habits to maintain good health. When meals are poorly planned or unhealthy eating habits are practised, they may affect the health and well-being of an individual.
A menu card is a plan that shows the meals to be prepared and eaten on different days of the week, usually from Monday to Sunday. It helps to organise meals, provide variety, save time, and reduce food wastage.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the effects of wrong meal planning, good and poor eating habits, and the meaning and importance of a menu card.
LESSON 1 - EFFECTS OF WRONG MEAL PLANNING
Wrong meal planning occurs when meals are planned without considering the nutritional needs, age, health condition, income, food availability, or preferences of the people who will eat them.
Effects include:
1. Poor nutrition.
2. Lack of essential nutrients.
3. Poor growth and development in children.
4. Weakness and tiredness.
5. Increased risk of illness.
6. Food wastage.
7. Unnecessary spending of money.
8. Lack of variety in meals.
LESSON 2 - MEANING OF EATING HABITS
Eating habits are the regular ways or practices through which a person chooses, prepares, and eats food.
Good eating habits include:
1. Eating a variety of nutritious foods.
2. Eating meals at regular times.
3. Eating fruits and vegetables regularly.
4. Drinking enough clean water.
5. Washing hands before eating.
6. Eating food in moderate amounts.
7. Avoiding excessive sugary, salty, and fatty foods.
EFFECTS OF POOR EATING HABITS
Poor eating habits can have negative effects on the body.
Effects include:
1. Poor growth and development.
2. Excessive weight gain or weight loss.
3. Weakness and tiredness.
4. Poor concentration in school.
5. Increased risk of diseases.
6. Poor dental health.
7. Nutritional deficiencies.
LESSON 3 - MEANING OF MENU CARD
A menu card is a plan that shows the different meals to be prepared and eaten on each day of the week, usually from Monday to Sunday.
Example of a Weekly Menu Card
Day - Breakfast - Lunch - Dinner
Monday - Bread and egg - Rice and vegetables - Beans and plantain
Tuesday - Pap and akara - Yam and vegetable sauce - Eba and soup
Wednesday - Oatmeal and milk - Beans and rice - Yam and egg sauce
Thursday - Bread and tea - Jollof rice and chicken - Beans and plantain
Friday - Pap and moi moi - Yam and vegetable sauce - Rice and vegetables
Saturday - Boiled yam and egg - Beans and plantain - Eba and soup
Sunday - Bread and egg - Rice, chicken and vegetables - Yam and egg sauce
IMPORTANCE OF A MENU CARD
1. It helps to organise meals for the week.
2. It ensures variety in meals.
3. It eelps provide balanced meals.
4. It saves time in meal preparation.
5. It helps control food expenses.
6. It reduces food wastage.
7. It takes shopping for food easier.

D. More energy

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Stitches are important in sewing because they help to join, hold, or decorate pieces of fabric. Different stitches are used for different purposes in sewing.
Some stitches are made temporarily and can be removed easily, while others are made to hold fabric permanently.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning and types of temporary and permanent stitches and their uses.
MEANING OF STITCHES
A stitch is a series of loops or passes of thread made with a needle to join, hold, or decorate pieces of fabric.
Stitches are mainly divided into temporary stitches and permanent stitches.
1. TEMPORARY STITCHES
Temporary stitches are stitches used to hold pieces of fabric together for a short time. They are usually removed after the permanent stitching has been completed.
Types of Temporary Stitches:
- Tacking stitch: Used to hold two or more pieces of fabric together temporarily.
- Even tacking: Made with stitches of equal length and spacing.
- Uneven tacking: Made with stitches of different lengths and spacing.
- Diagonal tacking: Made with diagonal stitches to hold layers of fabric in place.
2. PERMANENT STITCHES
Permanent stitches are stitches that are made to hold fabric together for a long time. They are not normally removed after sewing.
Types of Permanent Stitches:
- Running stitch: A simple stitch used for joining fabric and making seams.
- Backstitch: A strong stitch used for making firm seams.
- Overcasting stitch: Used to prevent the edges of fabric from fraying.
- Hemming stitch: Used to secure the folded edges of garments and other fabric items.
- Blanket stitch: Used mainly to finish and decorate fabric edges.
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN TEMPORARY AND PERMANENT STITCHES
1. Temporary stitches are used for a short period, while permanent stitches are used for a long period.
2. Temporary stitches are usually removed after use, while permanent stitches are usually not removed.
3. Temporary stitches hold fabric temporarily, while permanent stitches hold fabric firmly and permanently.
4. Examples of temporary stitches include tacking stitches, while examples of permanent stitches include running and backstitches.

INTRODUCTION

With simple sewing materials, pupils can use different stitches to produce useful articles such as handkerchiefs, table mats, small bags, and decorative fabric pieces.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the types and uses of stitches and practise using different stitches to produce simple articles.
TYPES AND USES OF STITCHES
1. Running Stitch
A running stitch is a simple permanent stitch made by passing the needle in and out of the fabric.
Use: It is used for joining pieces of fabric and making simple seams.
2. Backstitches
A backstitch is a strong permanent stitch in which each stitch overlaps the previous one.
Use: It is used for making strong and firm seams.
3. Overcasting Stitch
An overcasting stitch is made over the edge of fabric.
Use: It is used to prevent the edges of fabric from fraying.
4. Hemming Stitch
A hemming stitch is used to secure a folded edge of fabric.
Use: It is used for finishing the edges of clothes, handkerchiefs, table mats, and other articles.
5. Blanket Stitch
A blanket stitch is a decorative stitch made along the edge of fabric.
Use: It is used to finish and decorate fabric edges.
6. Tacking Stitch
A tacking stitch is a temporary stitch used to hold fabric together before permanent sewing.
Use: It is used to hold pieces of fabric in position temporarily.
ARTICLES THAT CAN BE PRODUCED USING DIFFERENT STITCHES
Pupils can use different types of stitches to produce simple articles such as:
1. Handkerchief: Running stitch and hemming stitch can be used to join and finish the edges.
2. Table mat: Running stitch and hemming stitch can be used for joining and finishing.
3. Small fabric bag: Running stitch and backstitch can be used to join the fabric firmly.
4. Decorative fabric: Blanket stitch can be used to finish and decorate the edges.
5. Simple apron: Running stitch and hemming stitch can be used for joining and finishing.
MATERIALS NEEDED FOR MAKING STITCHES
1. Needle - Used to pass the thread through the fabric.
2. Thread - Used to make stitches and join fabric.
3. Fabric - The material on which the stitches are made.
4. Scissors - Used to cut fabric and thread.
5. Thimble - Protects the finger when pushing the needle through fabric.
6. Measuring tape - Used to measure the fabric.
7. Tailor’s chalk - Used to mark measurements and cutting lines on fabric.
SIMPLE STEPS FOR PRODUCING AN ARTICLE
1. Select the article to be made.
2. Gather the necessary materials.
3. Measure and mark the fabric.
4. Cut the fabric according to the required size.
5. Join the pieces using the appropriate stitch.
6. Finish the edges neatly.

INTRODUCTION
Detergent is an important cleaning agent used to remove dirt, grease, and stains from clothes and surfaces. It can be produced by combining suitable ingredients in the correct proportions.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the materials and ingredients used for making detergent, the simple steps involved, and the safety precautions to observe during the process.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF DETERGENT
Detergent is a cleaning substance used to remove dirt, grease, stains, and other unwanted materials from clothes, floors, dishes, and other surfaces.
INGREDIENTS FOR MAKING DETERGENT
Common ingredients used in making simple powdered or liquid detergent include:
1. Soda ash - Helps to soften water and improve cleaning.
2. Sulphonic acid (LABSA) - Provides the main cleaning action in many detergent formulations.
3. Sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) - Used in some formulations to neutralise acidic ingredients.
4. Sodium silicate - Helps improve cleaning and supports the detergent mixture.
5. Sodium sulphate - May be used as a filler in powdered detergent.
6. Perfume - Gives the detergent a pleasant smell.

SAFETY PRECAUTIONS
Some detergent-making ingredients can be irritating or corrosive. Pupils should not handle concentrated chemicals such as caustic soda or sulphonic acid without trained adult supervision.
Important precautions include:
1. Wear protective gloves and other suitable protective equipment.
2. Avoid contact with the eyes and skin.
3. Do not taste or inhale the ingredients.
4. Work in a well-ventilated area.
5. Use clearly labelled containers.
6. Keep chemicals away from children and food.
7. Follow the manufacturer’s safety instructions for each chemical.
8. Wash hands thoroughly after the activity.
For Primary 6 practical work, it is safer to use a teacher-prepared or commercially supplied detergent base rather than allowing pupils to handle concentrated chemicals directly.
LESSON 3 - HOW TO MAKE DETERGENT
Simple steps to make detergent are as follows:
1. Gather the materials: Arrange all the materials and ingredients needed.
2. Measure the ingredients: Measure the detergent base and water as instructed.
3. Mix the base: Pour the prepared detergent base into a clean container.
4. Add water: Add the required amount of clean water gradually while stirring.
5. Add colour: Add a small amount of suitable colouring agent and mix well.
6. Add perfume: Add a suitable perfume and stir gently.
7. Mix thoroughly: Continue stirring until the mixture is evenly combined.
8. Package the detergent: Pour the finished detergent into clean bottles using a funnel.
9. Label and store: Label the bottles and store the detergent safely away from children and food.
Safety: Concentrated chemicals such as caustic soda and sulphonic acid should only be handled by a trained adult using appropriate protective equipment.
